front: What are the main ideas of the **particle model**?
back: All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving, with spaces between them and forces of attraction pulling them together.
Packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating in fixed positions. Fixed shape and volume.
Close together but jumbled, able to slide past each other. Fixed volume, but takes the shape of its container.
Far apart, moving quickly and randomly in all directions. Fills its container and is easy to squash.
Solid → liquid. The particles gain energy and break out of their fixed positions.
Liquid → solid. The particles lose energy and are pulled into fixed positions. It happens at the same temperature as melting.
Liquid → gas at the surface of a liquid. It can happen at any temperature.
Liquid → gas throughout the liquid, at the boiling point. Water boils at 100 °C at sea level.
Gas → liquid. The particles lose energy and come together, e.g. droplets on a cold mirror.
Solid → gas without becoming a liquid first, e.g. dry ice (solid carbon dioxide).
The spreading of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration, caused by their random movement.
Higher temperature → particles have more energy and move faster, so diffusion and evaporation speed up.

front: Why does the temperature stay the same while ice melts?
back: The energy goes into overcoming the forces between the particles, not into making them move faster.

front: Do particles get bigger when they are heated?
back: No. They move faster and spread further apart. The particles themselves stay the same size.
A property you can observe or measure without making a new substance, e.g. melting point, density, colour or conductivity.

front: How do you predict a substance's state from its melting and boiling points?
back: Below the melting point: solid. Between the melting and boiling points: liquid. Above the boiling point: gas.
Evaporation: only at the surface, at any temperature. Boiling: throughout the liquid, only at the boiling point.
